en: The Jātaka:
The Collection of Ten,
Chapter on the Four Gates (Catudvāravagga)
3. The Catuposathiya Jātaka:
“The noble person who does not harbor anger toward one who should be provoked to anger never becomes angry at any time.”
“Even when provoked, he does not manifest anger;
him indeed they call a *śramaṇa* in the world.
“He who, with a restrained belly, endures hunger,”
The self-controlled ascetic, moderate in food and drink,
commits no evil for the sake of nutriment;
him indeed they call a "recluse" (samaṇa) in the world.
“Having utterly abandoned all play and delight,
you do not speak any falsehood in the world;
you are detached from sexual intercourse, which is a ground for vanity.”
“Indeed, that man they call a *śramaṇa* in the world.
“He who, having fully understood all possessions and states of greed, completely relinquishes them;”
"One who is tamed, established in self, without 'mine-ness,' and free from longing—
him indeed they call a *śramaṇa* in the world.
"We ask the Maker of Unrivalled Wisdom,"
A dispute has arisen among us in our discourses;
cut through today our doubts and hesitations,
so that we may all cross over this doubt today.
“Those who are wise and possess insight into the meaning speak appropriately and at the right time.
How indeed could there be any fault in words that have not been spoken?”
"O lords of men, may the skilled ones lead us to the goal.
How indeed does the Naga king speak,
and what does the Garuda, the son of Vinatā, say?"
"But what does the King of the Gandhabbas say?
And how does the best of kings among the Kurus speak?
"The Naga king speaks indeed of patience."
The Garuḍa, son of Veṇatā, [praised] moderation in food;
the King of the Gandhabbas, the relinquishing of delight;
and the best of kings among the Kurus, nothingness.”
“All these are well-spoken;
herein there is nothing ill-spoken.
And that upon which they are established—”
Like spokes well-fastened to the hub,
he who is endowed with these four qualities—
him indeed they call a *samaṇa* in the world.
“You indeed are the best, you are unsurpassed;
you are the guardian of Dhamma, the knower of Dhamma, the one of excellent wisdom.
Having grasped the question with wisdom, [you have answered].”
The steadfast one has cut through doubts;
he has severed uncertainty and all hesitations,
just as Cunda cuts an elephant’s tusk with a saw.
This garment, blue-lotus-hued, stainless, priceless, and smoke-colored—
being satisfied by the answer to my question, [I offer it].
I give to you, O wise one, as an offering of Dhamma,
a golden garland blooming with a hundred petals,
complete with filaments and adorned with a thousand jewels.
Satisfied by the answer to my question,
O wise one, I give this jewel to you as an offering of Dharma—
priceless, beautiful, and radiant.
This jewel-adorned necklace hanging from my neck,
O wise one, I give to you as an offering of Dhamma, satisfied by your answer to my question.
A thousand cows and a bull-nāga,
and ten chariots yoked with thoroughbreds— these I give,
satisfied by your answer to the question.
“I give you sixteen excellent cows.
At that time, Sāriputta was the nāga and Kolita was the supaṇṇa.
King Anuruddha the Gandhabba,
King Ānanda the Wise,
and the Bodhisatta Vidhura.
"Thus you should remember this Jātaka.
This is the third, the Catuposathiya Jātaka.
